description_full: Jones Lang LaSalle Incorporated operates as a commercial real estate and investment management company. It engages in buying, building, occupying, managing, and investing in office, industrial, hotel, multi-family, retail and data center properties in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. The company also offers agency leasing, tenant representation, property management, advisory, and consulting services; and debt advisory, loan sales and servicing, value and risk advisory, equity and funds placement, merger and acquisition, corporate advisory, and investment sales and advisory services. In addition, it provides on-site real estate management services for office, industrial, retail, multifamily residential, and other properties; cloud-based software solutions; integrated facilities management, space planning, office design, and workplace strategy consulting services; program and project management, implementation and support, managed services, and advisory/consulting services; and investment management services to institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals, as well as designing, building, management, and consulting services to tenants of leased space, owners in self-occupied buildings, and owners of real estate investments. It provides its services to real estate owners, occupiers, investors, and developers for various property types, including critical environments and data centers, offices, industrial and warehouses, residential properties, infrastructure projects, retail and shopping malls, logistics, and military housing and transportation centers; and hotels and hospitality, cultural, educational, government, healthcare and laboratory, and sports facilities. The company was formerly known as LaSalle Partners Incorporated and changed its name to Jones Lang LaSalle Incorporated in March 1999. Jones Lang LaSalle Incorporated was incorporated in 1997 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Jones Lang LaSalle Incorporated is a large-cap real estate business with a $16.8B market cap on $26.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $978M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.51× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 9.3×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 1.18, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.55 vs 5y 1.24), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades 31% below its DCF fair value of $532, a meaningful margin of safety.

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 21% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.6% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 10.0%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.18).

Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.51x.

hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.8% over 3 years and 9.5% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 64%).

Free cash flow has compounded 0.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue up 16% and FFO growth of 1.4% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 0.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and institutions hold 100%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $4.0M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.3% (1.3% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 113,200 employees, each generates about $231K of revenue, 0.1x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 15.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $9K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.7M (21x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
